ta-l1d14q3-d1e3501.summary: Opens the question of from whom the Spirit proceeds temporally, specifically whether holy people can give the Spirit (other points are deferred to Dist. 16). First argument that they can: remission of sins happens only through the Spirit, and holy people can remit sins ('whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven', John 20:23).
claims: Holy people can remit sins, which happens only through the Spirit.

ta-l1d14q3-d1e3507.summary: Second argument. The Spirit's grace is like spiritual light, and one body illuminated by bodily light can illuminate another, so one in grace can confer grace on another.
claims: One illuminated body can illuminate another.

ta-l1d14q3-d1e3510.summary: Third argument. One who gives the occasion of harm is held to have done the harm, so one who does something upon which the Spirit's grace is conferred seems to confer it. Ministers of the Church dispense the sacraments, in which the Spirit's grace is given.
claims: Giving the occasion of an effect counts as causing it.

ta-l1d14q3-d1e3514.summary: Sed contra. A giver is never inferior to what is given, and every minister of the Church is inferior to the Spirit and like his instrument.
claims: The giver is not inferior to the gift.

ta-l1d14q3-d1e3517.summary: Second sed contra. The Spirit is given only in sanctifying grace, which no creature can confer, since nothing infinite comes from a finite power, and grace has a kind of infinite power, joining us to the infinite God.
claims: Grace, as joining us to the infinite God, cannot come from a finite power.

ta-l1d14q3-d1e3520.summary: Thomas's determination: no creature can give the Spirit; God alone can. Temporal procession involves two relations, the eternal one by which the Spirit goes out from Father and Son and the temporal one arising because the creature, through a gift received, stands in a new way toward him, and neither can come from a creature. No creature is the source of the eternal relation. Nor can any creature confer sanctifying grace, in which alone the Spirit is given, for three reasons. (1) Every creaturely operation presupposes the potency of matter, so no creature can produce a form not educed from the potency of matter, which is why the rational soul is created by God alone; grace raises a person above all natural being, eliciting acts and ordering to an end nature cannot reach, so it is not educed from matter and is conferred by God alone. (2) Every action is according to some likeness, each agent producing its like, so a perfection that joins someone immediately to another as that other's likeness must be produced immediately by it; grace joins us to God himself without a creaturely medium, so it must proceed immediately from God. (3) From grace's power, which elicits meritorious acts leading to the infinite good, and from the principle that in agents ordered as principal and instrument the ultimate perfection is attributed to the first agent, as substantial form comes not from fire's heat, its instrument, but from the heavenly power.
claims: God alone can give the Holy Spirit.
Sanctifying grace cannot be produced by any creature, since it is not educed from matter, joins us immediately to God, and leads to the infinite good.
In ordered agents, the ultimate perfection is attributed to the first agent.

ta-l1d14q3-d1e3523.summary: Reply to the first argument. Ministers of the Church do not remit sins by authority or as efficient causes; God alone does ('I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake', Isa. 43:25). They remit by ministry, so they can be called ministers of the conferral of the Spirit but not givers, since giving implies authority.
claims: Ministers remit sins and confer the Spirit by ministry, not by authority.

ta-l1d14q3-d1e3529.summary: Reply to the second argument. Spiritual light is nobler and more powerful than bodily light, and by its dignity it cannot be produced by any creature, like the rational soul.
claims: Spiritual light, like the rational soul, can be produced only by God.

ta-l1d14q3-d1e3532.summary: Reply to the third argument. One who gives the occasion of harm is held to have done harm only interpretively, not properly, and still does something proportioned and sufficient for the harm to follow. But no operation of a minister, considered in itself as coming from the minister, is proportioned and sufficient for the giving of the Spirit to follow; it has this only from divine institution and condescension. So all the causality is referred to God.
claims: Sacramental ministry is not of itself proportioned to the giving of the Spirit; its efficacy comes from divine institution.

ta-l1d14q3-d1e3541.summary: An expositio textus on Distinction 14. (1) 'Not separately from the Father into the Son and from the Son into the creature' seems to contradict the two processions of Distinction 13, but they are not simply two: one includes the other, and the words also imply that the Father spirates the Spirit immediately as the Son does, not only in power but as a supposit, like two people acting together. (2) Christ's breathing showed that the Spirit also proceeds from him. One might object that the Spirit is temporally given by himself too, without being from himself. When the Spirit is said to give himself, this refers to the gift in which he is given, not to the proceeding person, since he is not from himself as an originating principle. But the bodily breath signified that the person of the Spirit proceeds from the Son. (3) 'He is the power that went out from him' seems wrong, since power is appropriated to the Son. Power can be appropriated to all three under different aspects: to the Father as pertaining to the perfection of might, to the Son as the mean between essence and operation, as the Father works through the Son, and to the Spirit as it makes the work and the worker good, goodness being appropriated to him, or as to its effect, a benefit freely given, whose reason is love.
claims: The temporal procession includes the eternal; the Father spirates immediately as a supposit.
The Spirit gives himself only as to the gift, not as an originating principle of his own person.
Power is appropriated to Father, Son, and Spirit under different aspects.

ta-l1d14q3-Dd1e3493.summary: Article 1 (the only article) asks whether holy people can give the Holy Spirit. Thomas holds that God alone can. Neither the eternal relation nor the temporal one, which arises through sanctifying grace, can come from a creature. Sanctifying grace is not educed from matter, joins us immediately to God as his likeness, and leads to the infinite good, so it is produced by God alone, as the ultimate perfection is attributed to the first agent. Ministers of the Church remit sins and confer the Spirit by ministry, not authority, and the sacraments' efficacy for giving the Spirit comes wholly from divine institution.
claims: God alone can give the Holy Spirit; ministers confer him only by ministry.
Sanctifying grace can be created only by God.

ta-l1d14q3-Dd1e3536.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 14 explains that the Spirit's procession is not 'divided' into stages and that the Father spirates immediately. It interprets Christ's breathing as showing the Spirit's procession from the Son and assigns the appropriation of 'power' to each person under a different aspect.
claims: The Father spirates immediately; power is appropriated to each person under different aspects.

ta-l1d14q3.summary: Quaestio 3 of Book I, Distinction 14 asks from whom the Spirit's temporal procession comes, and in particular whether holy people can give the Spirit. Thomas holds that God alone gives him. Sanctifying grace, the only gift in which the Spirit is given, is not educed from matter, joins us immediately to God, and orders us to the infinite good, so it can be produced only by God. Ministers of the Church act by ministry, not authority, and sacraments have their efficacy from divine institution. The Expositio explains the immediacy of the Father's spiration, the significance of Christ's breathing, and the appropriation of power to each person.
claims: God alone gives the Holy Spirit, since only he can create sanctifying grace.
Ministers and sacraments are instruments whose efficacy derives from divine institution.
